content: Toward the end of the 19th century, scientists began to recognize the significant role ticks could play as vectors for transmitting diseases. By the late 20th century, several tick-borne diseases, including babesiosis, Lyme disease, and ehrlichiosis, were identified in the United States. Ehrlichiosis is caused by various bacterial species within the genus Ehrlichia (pronounced err-lick-ee-uh), which were first recognized in 1935. Over time, veterinary pathogens causing diseases in animals such as dogs, cattle, sheep, goats, and horses were also identified. Currently, three species of Ehrlichia in the United States and one in Japan are known to cause disease in humans. It is possible that additional species may be identified in the future as diagnostic methods improve. The first human Ehrlichia pathogen was identified in Japan in 1953. This pathogen, Ehrlichia sennetsu, causes a condition known as sennetsu fever, which is characterized by fever and swollen lymph nodes. Sennetsu fever is rare outside of the Far East and Southeast Asia, with most cases reported in western Japan. In the United States, human diseases caused by Ehrlichia species have been recognized since the mid-1980s. Ehrlichioses represent a group of clinically similar but epidemiologically and etiologically distinct diseases caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, Ehrlichia ewingii, and a bacterium closely related or identical to Ehrlichia phagocytophila. The focus of this discussion will be on the types of ehrlichiosis that occur in the United States. Human ehrlichiosis caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis was first described in 1987. This disease primarily occurs in the southeastern and south-central regions of the United States and is transmitted by the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum). Human granulocytic ehrlichiosis (HGE), the second recognized ehrlichial infection in humans in the United States, was first described in 1994. The causative species of HGE has not been formally named but is closely related or identical to the veterinary pathogens Ehrlichia equi and Ehrlichia phagocytophila. HGE is transmitted by the blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis) and the western blacklegged tick (Ixodes pacificus) in the United States. Ehrlichia ewingii is the most recently recognized human pathogen. Disease caused by E. ewingii has been reported in a limited number of patients in Missouri, Oklahoma, and Tennessee, most of whom had underlying immunosuppression. The full geographic range of this species, its vectors, and its role in human disease are still under investigation. The early clinical presentations of ehrlichiosis can resemble nonspecific signs and symptoms of various other infectious and non-infectious diseases. It is unclear whether all individuals infected with Ehrlichia bacteria become ill. Many infected individuals may develop such mild symptoms that they do not seek medical attention, or they may remain entirely asymptomatic. The diagnosis of ehrlichiosis is based on a combination of clinical signs and symptoms and confirmatory laboratory tests. Blood samples can be sent to reference laboratories for testing, although the availability of different types of laboratory tests varies significantly. Laboratory findings indicative of ehrlichiosis include low white blood cell count, low platelet count, and elevated liver enzymes. Appropriate antibiotic treatment should be initiated immediately when there is a strong suspicion of ehrlichiosis based on clinical and epidemiologic findings. Treatment should not be delayed while awaiting laboratory confirmation. Fever typically subsides within 24–72 hours after treatment with doxycycline or other tetracyclines. A lack of rapid response to tetracycline antibiotics argues against a diagnosis of ehrlichiosis. Preventative therapy in asymptomatic individuals with recent tick bites is not recommended. Reducing exposure to ticks is the most effective way to prevent ehrlichial infection. For individuals exposed to tick-infested environments, prompt and careful inspection and removal of crawling or attached ticks is a critical preventive measure. Transmission of microorganisms from the tick to the host may require several hours of attachment.
